Incorporating the April 2020 Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS), the tone of the April 29, 2020 FOMC statement skews further negative. SLOOS reports broad-based tightening in bank lending standards and terms—on C&I loans and across CRE segments (nonfarm nonresidential, multifamily, construction/land development)—including wider loan rate spreads, higher costs of credit lines, lower loan-to-value ratios, and stricter credit policies. Banks cite the deteriorating economic outlook, COVID-19–related industry problems, heightened risk aversion, and liquidity needs as key reasons; many also expect further tightening ahead. Demand indicators are mixed but generally soft in risk-sensitive areas (weaker for nonfarm nonresidential and construction/land development), with some offset from stronger demand for government-backed residential mortgages and increased borrower inquiries. Net effect: credit supply is constricting as the economy weakens, reinforcing the FOMC’s assessment of “considerable risks” and “impaired” credit flow. While the Fed’s QE in Treasuries and agency MBS/CMBS and large-scale repo operations support market functioning, SLOOS suggests transmission to households and businesses remains challenged.

Compared with the prior FSR-based read, SLOOS evidence of active and prospective tightening in bank credit conditions warrants a modestly more negative stance.
